newsitem.title: UK: Britain opens inquiry into N.Irish jobs row.
newsitem.headline: Britain opens inquiry into N.Irish jobs row.

text.p: An independent investigator said on Tuesday he will try to establish the facts behind a row that has sparked Catholic demands for the resignation of a British Northern Ireland minister, Baroness Jean Denton.

Maurice Hayes said that he would investigate the circumstances in which a Catholic official was transferred from her job as Denton's diary secretary. Media reports said she was later found to have been subjected to sectarian harassment by the minister's private secretary.
Agriculture and Economy Minister Denton is under pressure to quit by politicians who accuse her of mishandling the case and ignoring "fair employment" guidelines for the British-ruled province.
But Denton says she has done nothing wrong and she has "no intention of resigning".
Hayes, appointed by Britain late on Monday, said he would conduct a fact finding inquiry into the agriculture department's employment policies.

"The big question is: who did what? At the moment I don't know who did what and I have an open mind," he told BBC radio, adding that he would investigate whether sectarian considerations were involved in staff deployment.

Denton says the transfer of her diary secretary was an efficiency move which was not linked to a complaint that the Catholic woman later lodged against Denton's private secretary for sectarian harassment arising out of an incident in July 1995.
She was subsequently awarded 10,000 pounds ($16,000) and received an apology from the Department of Agriculture.
Sir Patrick Mayhew, Britain's chief minister for the province, defended Denton on Monday against "unjust criticism".

Nationalist politicians, whose Catholic constitutents have been shown by official figures to be much more likely than Protestants to be unemployed, accused Denton of ignoring a code laid down by Britain to ease imbalances in the workforce.

Catholic parties called for Denton to quit on Sunday after the BBC reported she had ignored guidelines in a second unrelated case when she appointed a new travelling secretary who had not been short-listed for the job.

Sinn Fein, the political arm of the Irish Republican Army, said discrimination against Catholics was in-built in the province and said it would raise the controversy with politicians in Washington and New York this week.
